1:
Clarke will not begin until the authorship is settled, and he settles it against Moses. This chapter could not have been written by him, for a man certainly cannot give an account of his own death and burial; to suppose that these circumstances were shown him by especial revelation is departing far from propriety. He therefore believes the twelve verses should be the first chapter of Joshua, of which they are an evident continuation, and quotes an intelligent Jew on how easily this could have happened: most commentators think Ezra the author, some Joshua, others the seventy elders; and in those early ages books were connected together on the same roll, so the beginning of one might be transferred to the end of another and in time be taken for its conclusion. Calvin raises the same question and refuses to spend anything on it: it is not certain who wrote the chapter, unless we admit the conjecture of the ancients that Joshua did; but since Eleazar the priest might have done it, better to leave a matter of no great importance undecided.

On the ascent itself Calvin and Henry agree and press the same point. Calvin says the ascent was equivalent to a voluntary going forth to death, since being called by God to die he went to meet death of his own accord; such willing submission proceeded from no other source than faith in God's grace. Naturally it must have been an awful thing to him as to anyone else, but the testimony of grace being interposed he offers himself without alarm. Henry adds what nobody else notices, that he went up alone and without help, a sign that his natural force was not abated, since he could walk up a high hill without the supporters he had once needed when his hands were heavy; and alone without company, for having taken leave of Joshua and Eleazar at the foot of the hill he gave them such a charge as Abraham gave his servants at the foot of another — tarry you here while I go yonder and die. They must not see him die, because they must not know his sepulchre.

That he saw the whole land at all is agreed to be miraculous. Henry reckons Canaan at fifty or sixty miles from end to end and says his sight, good as it was, could not have reached it unless miraculously assisted and enlarged; all the prospects we have of the better country we are beholden to grace for, since God gives the eye as well as the object. Calvin grants that some have been endued with incredible powers of vision, but finds the peculiarity elsewhere: Moses distinctly examined every portion as if he had been really on the spot, the vision being otherwise useless unless he beheld the future habitation of the people. Henry alone suspects an imitation, thinking the devil designed to mimic this sight and to out-do it when he showed our Saviour all the kingdoms of the world from an exceeding high mountain, not gradually as here, first one country and then another, but all in a moment of time.

Wesley reads the panorama as a compass, the quarters named standing for all the rest, the utmost sea being the midland sea, the western bound of the land of promise. He alone stops over the city of palm trees, which is Jericho, so called from the multitude of palm trees in those parts, as Josephus and Strabo write, and named from the balm growing there, a word signifying odoriferous or sweet smelling. Ellicott alone weighs what God says while he shows it. One Jewish comment makes the purpose of the sight to be that Moses might tell Abraham, Isaac and Jacob that the oath sworn to them was performed; but in Paradise, he answers, they scarcely needed Moses to tell them of it.
5:
That Moses died at all needed defending. Gill reports that some Jewish writers affirm, against the express words of the text, that he died not but was translated, being an angel and unable to die; he answers that Moses did die, for the servants of the Lord die as well as others, and quotes their own saying — Moses died, and who shall not die? What at the mouth of the Lord means divides the rest. Wesley takes the rabbinic reading without hesitation: the Jews say God sucked his soul out of his body with a kiss, and no doubt he died in the embraces of his love. Henry reports the same saying and declines it, allowing that Moses no doubt died very easily, a delightful death with no bands in it, but holding that the phrase means no more than that he died in compliance with the will of God. Ellicott is sharper: hence the interpretation that he died by a kiss, but the language of the narrative is too simple to need even that, since it had been the habit of Moses for years to do everything at the mouth of the Lord, and this was one last act of obedience. Clarke adds a possibility nobody else raises, that the words may refer only to the sentence of exclusion passed at Meribah.

On the burial Calvin and Henry disagree about the undertakers. Calvin rejects both the rendering that he was buried and the rendering that he buried himself, since those who shrink from assigning the office to God are avoiding an absurdity which does not exist; and having assigned it to God he refuses the usual softening, for there was no need to call in angels, since the earth would instantly have obeyed its Creator. Henry assigns it to God by the ministry of angels, which made the funeral, though very private, yet very magnificent. Gill, who lays out the range of opinion without settling it, guesses at Michael, who is no other than our Lord Jesus Christ. Why it was hidden they agree about: Clarke, lest the Israelites, prone to idolatry, should pay him divine honours; Calvin, because it was usual with the Jews, and a custom for which Christ reproves them, to kill the prophets and then reverence their tombs. On the contention of Michael with the devil, Henry thinks the devil would have made the place known that it might be a snare, and that those who give divine honours to relics side with the devil against Michael our prince. Ellicott has always believed something else: that it was a struggle for the body itself, Moses being about to be raised and Satan resisting his resurrection, since he and Elijah both appeared in glory on the holy mount and the New Testament makes no difference between them.

The unimpaired old age they treat as a public mercy rather than a personal one. Calvin observes that by then the vigour of the race had so diminished that after seventy men dragged out their life in labour and sorrow; had the powers of Moses failed before the entrance into the land his debility would have been inconvenient to the people, so that in not suffering him to fail God consulted their welfare. Henry divides the hundred and twenty into three forties — a courtier at ease in Pharaoh's court, a poor desolate shepherd in Midian, a king in Jeshurun encumbered with care — and turns the undimmed eye upon the law itself, whose eye is not waxen dim nor its force abated. On the thirty days Calvin notes that the ancients were particular in their funeral rites because their faith was not yet elevated enough to forego such aids — a ceremony ended with the shadows of the Law, our dead being now buried so that grief may be restrained by the hope of the resurrection.
9:
Henry opens with a caution about how to praise the dead: it is ungrateful so to magnify our living friends as to forget the merits of those that are gone, and unjust so to cry up those that are gone as to despise the benefit we have in those that survive. He then lists three things that cleared Joshua's call. God fitted him, for he was full of the spirit of wisdom, and he had need who had such a peevish people to rule and such a politic people to conquer, conduct being as requisite in a general as courage. Moses ordained him by laying on hands, which is why God gave him a more than ordinary spirit of wisdom. And the people cheerfully owned him, so that when Moses died they were not as sheep having no shepherd. Calvin adds that Joshua had been previously endowed with excellent gifts but was now more splendidly adorned with the ensigns of dignity, in order that his calling by God might be more certainly proved, the imposition of hands being no empty symbol of grace. Ellicott notices two things nobody else does: that this is the first example of ordination in Holy Scripture, and that the people did as the Lord commanded Moses, not as he commanded Joshua — Joshua would not separate himself from the law given by his master.

Whether the closing eulogy is absolute or bounded is the question of the last three verses. Calvin says the eulogy seems added that the children of Abraham might depend on Moses until the manifestation of Christ, the superiority remaining with him lest they decline in the smallest degree from the rule of the Law. Clarke says all this continued true till the advent of Jesus Christ, of whom Moses said that a prophet should be raised up like unto him — but how great was this person compared with Moses, who desired to see God's glory and could not bear the sight, seeing only his back parts, whereas Jesus, in whom dwells all the fullness of the Godhead, has declared God to man. Gill runs the same line through the candidates for the authorship: no such prophet arose in the times of Joshua, who the Jews say wrote at least the last eight verses, nor of Samuel, whom others take for the writer, nor of Ezra, nor in the whole Old Testament dispensation. He grants that the Jews themselves own the Messiah equal to Moses or above him, though of all other prophets they call Moses the prince and father. Ellicott alone reads the verse as evidence about the writer rather than about Christ, judging the words later than the time of Joshua, when longer experience had shown men how far inferior the prophets were to their great predecessor.

What the incomparability consists in is disputed in one word. Henry takes the knowing to run both ways: God knew him face to face, and so he knew God; and where other prophets were struck with terror when God appeared, Moses preserved his tranquillity whenever he received a revelation. Keil will not have it: whom Jehovah knew, not who knew him. Calvin names two signs of the excellency, the familiar acquaintance with God and the glory of the miracles, holding that Moses beheld that glory not in its perfection but beyond all others. Henry ends where Clarke does: as far as the other prophets came short of Moses, our Lord went beyond him, his doctrine more excellent and his communion with the Father more intimate, for he had lain in his bosom from eternity; Moses was faithful as a servant, but Christ as a Son; and the history of Moses leaves him buried in the plains of Moab, where that of our Saviour leaves him at the right hand of the Majesty on high, of whose government there shall be no end.
